Living Well / Proposed experiment

Proposed experiment: does a household system remove more work than it adds?

Proposed experiment · 3 min read · Published October 8, 2026

On this page
  1. Choose a low-stakes shared inconvenience
  2. Write down the simplest alternative
  3. Count the work that the new arrangement creates
  4. Ask whether it fits an ordinary busy day
  5. Report a decision, not a success story
  6. One question to take with you

A system can look organized while quietly creating more work. Test the whole arrangement, including who maintains it and who has to adapt.

Status: proposed experiment. This is a ready-to-try plan, not a completed trial, personal result, or claim of effectiveness. No findings are being reported.

Choose a low-stakes shared inconvenience

This plan has not been carried out as a reported field study. Select one repeated, low-risk situation and ask the people involved whether they want to try a change. Do not introduce monitoring or collect private information about household members.

Describe the current process fairly. What goes wrong, how often is it noticed, and who handles the repair? Include the possibility that the inconvenience is small enough that a new system is unnecessary.

Write down the simplest alternative

Before adding automation, consider one shared note, a label, or a clearer agreement. Choose a change that everyone can understand and reverse. A method that requires the most organized person to maintain a complex database is not automatically a household improvement.

State what would count as useful before beginning. It might be fewer missed items, less confusion about ownership, or less time spent searching. Keep the measure close to the original problem rather than adding an elaborate scorecard.

Count the work that the new arrangement creates

Record setup, learning, checking, updating, and repair. Include work done by people other than you. If AI contributes a checklist or organization scheme, count the effort required to verify and adapt it.

Avoid safety-critical trials. Do not experiment with medication, food-safety procedures, electrical work, home access, or emergency arrangements using this guide. The point is to examine a modest convenience, not to test whether a consequential shortcut happens to work.

Ask whether it fits an ordinary busy day

Use the system on a few real occasions, noting unusual circumstances. Ask the people involved whether it is understandable, useful, and fair. A method that works only when everyone remembers to maintain it may not solve a problem that began with remembering.

Keep missed attempts and workarounds in the record. They are part of the result, not blemishes to edit away. Stop or simplify the change when it creates conflict, exposes private information, or requires more attention than the problem warrants.

Report a decision, not a success story

A future field note should explain whether the household kept, changed, or abandoned the system and why. Mixed results deserve a plain account: something may have become clearer while maintenance became less acceptable.

Use the small-experiment worksheet privately. These observations could guide another local attempt, but they would not establish a general productivity benefit or show that technology caused every change noticed.

One optional practice

Agree on one reversible low-stakes change and a review point. Include everyone's maintenance effort. Treat a decision to return to a simpler method as a legitimate outcome.

Keep any notes privately. Skip or adapt this exercise if it does not fit your circumstances.

One question to take with you

Who does less work because of this system, and who does more?
